lead: A flywheel is a heavy rotating wheel that stores kinetic energy. An engine delivers torque in pulses and a punching press needs a large burst of energy for a moment in each stroke; the flywheel absorbs the surplus when supply exceeds demand and gives it back when demand exceeds supply, so the speed stays within limits. Its size is set by the energy it must swing and the speed variation allowed; its rim and arms must then survive the centrifugal and bending stresses of spinning.
prereq: You need kinetic energy of rotation, centrifugal force and bending stress from the chapters on stresses.

sections.h3: Energy fluctuation and the coefficient of speed fluctuation

blocks.text: Plot the engine torque against crank angle: this is the turning moment diagram. The mean torque line cuts it into loops; each loop's area is energy gained (above the line) or lost (below). Add the loop areas in turn: the difference between the largest and smallest running totals is the maximum fluctuation of energy ΔE.

blocks.where: C<sub>s</sub> is the coefficient of fluctuation of speed; ω₁ and ω₂ the largest and smallest speeds; ω = (ω₁ + ω₂)/2 the mean speed in rad/s. Engines need about 0.002 to 0.03; punching presses accept 0.05 to 0.2.
ΔE in J; I the mass moment of inertia in kg·m²; for a thin rim I ≈ mR², so ΔE = mv²C<sub>s</sub> with v = ωR the rim speed in m/s.

blocks.text: The ratio ΔE / (work done per cycle) is the coefficient of fluctuation of energy C<sub>e</sub>.

A solid disc of radius R and thickness b has I = ½mR² with m = ρπR²b. It is compact and cheap for small engines and presses. Its largest stress is at the centre, where the radial and hoop stresses are equal:

blocks.where: σ<sub>max</sub> in Pa; ν is Poisson's ratio (about 0.25 for cast iron); ρ in kg/m³. A cast-iron disc of R = 0.4 m at 600 rpm reaches only 1.85 MPa.

sections.h3: Rimmed flywheels: rim and arm stresses

blocks.text: A rimmed flywheel puts most of its mass in a heavy rim joined to the hub by arms, so it gives about twice the inertia of a disc of the same mass and radius. The arms and hub add only a small part, so they are usually neglected in finding the rim mass.

items: Hoop stress in a free rim: σt = ρv². It depends only on rim speed, so the material sets a safe speed: cast iron is usually kept below about 30 to 40 m/s.

Bending of the rim between arms: each segment acts as a beam fixed at the arms and loaded by its own centrifugal force, giving σb = 19.74ρv²R/(n²t), where n is the number of arms and t the radial thickness of the rim.
Combined rim stress (the usual textbook rule): σ = 0.75σ<sub>t</sub> + 0.25σ<sub>b</sub>.

Arms act as cantilevers from the hub carrying the torque T: the force at the rim is T/(nR), so the moment at the hub end is M = T(R − r)/(nR), with r the hub radius. Arms are usually elliptical, major axis a = 2 × minor axis, with Z = πa³/64 in the plane of rotation.

examples.question: A press punches 20 mm holes in 15 mm plate of ultimate shear strength 350 MPa, 30 holes a minute. Punching takes one-tenth of each cycle. The flywheel has a rim of mean radius 0.5 m, runs at 300 rpm, and its speed may fall by 10 % (C<sub>s</sub> = 0.1). Cast iron, ρ = 7200 kg/m³. Find the energy per hole, the flywheel's ΔE, the rim mass and cross-section, and the motor power.
steps: Energy per hole (force falling linearly to zero over the thickness): E = ½ × 329 900 × 0.015 = 2474 J.
The motor supplies this evenly over the cycle, so during the punch it gives only 1/10 of it. The flywheel must supply ΔE = 2474 × (1 − 1/10) = 2227 J.
Rim area: A = m/(ρ·2πR) = 90.2/(7200 × 3.142) = 0.00399 m² = 3990 mm², for example 80 mm × 50 mm.
Hoop stress: ρv² = 7200 × 15.71² = 1.78 MPa. Motor power: 2474 × 30/60 = 1237 W.
examples.answer: 2474 J per hole, ΔE = 2227 J, rim 90 kg of 3990 mm² section, hoop stress 1.78 MPa, motor about 1.24 kW (before losses).

examples.question: An engine flywheel must handle ΔE = 15 kJ at 600 rpm with C<sub>s</sub> = 0.02. Rim mean radius 0.6 m, radial thickness 120 mm, 6 elliptical arms, hub radius 0.1 m, cast iron ρ = 7200 kg/m³. The engine gives 50 kW. Find the rim mass and width, the rim stresses, and the arm size for a permissible stress of 15 MPa.
examples.answer: Rim 528 kg, 162 mm × 120 mm; rim stress 14.7 MPa; arms elliptical 56 mm × 28 mm at the hub.

traps: Using I = ½mR² for a rimmed wheel. That is the solid-disc value; a thin rim has I ≈ mR².
Taking the full punching energy as ΔE. The motor keeps supplying during the punch, so the flywheel supplies E(1 − punching fraction of the cycle).
Using diameter for R in v = ωR and m = I/R².
Leaving speed in rpm. Convert to rad/s (or v in m/s) before using ΔE = Iω²C<sub>s</sub>.
Checking only hoop stress. Rim bending between the arms is usually larger: 28.1 against 10.2 MPa in the second example.

quiz.q: Define the coefficient of fluctuation of speed.
quiz.a: C<sub>s</sub> = (ω₁ − ω₂)/ω, the range of speed divided by the mean speed.

quiz.q: How does a flywheel differ from a governor?
quiz.a: A flywheel limits the speed variation within each cycle by storing and releasing energy; it cannot change the mean speed. A governor changes the fuel supply to hold the mean speed when the load changes over many cycles.

quiz.q: The loops of a turning moment diagram are +600, −900, +700, −500, +400 and −300 J in order. Find ΔE.
A flywheel must absorb 8 kJ at 50 rad/s with C<sub>s</sub> = 0.04. Find I.
A cast-iron rim of mean radius 0.5 m runs at 900 rpm. Find v and the hoop stress (ρ = 7200 kg/m³).
quiz.a: v = 94.25 × 0.5 = 47.1 m/s; σ<sub>t</sub> = 7200 × 47.1² = 16.0 MPa. The speed is above the usual cast-iron limit, so steel would be safer.

quiz.q: Why is a rimmed flywheel lighter than a solid disc for the same ΔE, speed and outer size?
quiz.a: ΔE = Iω²C<sub>s</sub> fixes I. A rim has I ≈ mR², a disc only ½mR², because much of the disc's mass is near the axis where it moves slowly. The rim needs about half the mass.

beyond: Not for the exam. Flywheel energy storage systems spin carbon-fibre rotors at tens of thousands of rpm in vacuum on magnetic bearings, to smooth power for grids, data centres and trains. Dual-mass flywheels in cars split the flywheel with springs to cut driveline vibration. Search for flywheel energy storage and dual-mass flywheel.

figure.caption: The engine flywheel of the second worked example: a 528 kg cast-iron rim of 600 mm mean radius on six elliptical arms, turning at 37.7 m/s at the rim. Bending of the rim between the arms (28.1 MPa) is larger than the hoop stress (10.2 MPa).
